$comment: Accept/reject oracle for the TOP-LEVEL BLOCK GRAMMAR of a .chiplet document (docs/CHIPLET_FORMAT_SPEC.md, 'Top-level block grammar'). The grammar answers one question on the raw text, never on a parsed node tree: which run of lines belongs to which top-level key. Flow rule 4 (a host re-emits a flow block it did not author byte for byte) is defined in terms of it, and three implementations run THIS file rather than being compared to each other: the merge splitter in the KiCad plugin (chiplet_merge.split_top_level_blocks), the Python reference (chiplet_format_io.top_level_blocks) and the C++ reference (ChipletDocument::flow_yaml). Add a case here, never in a consumer. key_lines: 'line' is LINE CONTENT, i.e. the text up to the next LF with one optional trailing CR already removed; 'key' is capture group 1 of ^([A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*):(?:\\s.*)? anchored at both ends. Anchoring note, the same one adapter_id_cases.json carries: end the expression with \\Z in Python re or (?![\\s\\S]) portably, or match the whole content (std::regex_match); $ is WRONG in Python (it also matches before a trailing newline). ECMAScript's . excludes CR as well as LF, so a std::regex implementation writes [^\\n] where the expression writes . ; on a line the two mean the same thing. splits: 'doc' is the whole document text and 'blocks' is the exact slice per top-level key in document order, key line included, line endings untouched, nothing normalised. The empty key is the PREAMBLE (lines before the first key line). Concatenating every slice in order reproduces 'doc' byte for byte, which is the property that makes the grammar lossless, and every split case has it: the one case that did not (a repeated top-level key, whose two runs joined under the first occurrence) is now a refuse case. A case with "loadable": false is a splitter-only document that no reader is required to load. THE THREE VERDICTS ARE INDEPENDENT, and confusing them is the defect this file now pins: a document can be loadable and not splittable, and splittable and not writable. refuse: documents a SPLITTER refuses, each tagged with its "kind". A quoted key at column zero is valid YAML but is NOT a key line, so a splitter would attach its block to the preceding key, where that key's owner regenerates it away on the next re-export; splitting is refused instead of mis-attributing. "loads" says whether a READER still loads the document: true for the quoted key (flow rule 1 forbids rejecting a document over a block a host cannot handle), false for a repeated top-level key, where no reading is conforming at all because PyYAML takes the last value and yaml-cpp the first. A "forbidden_line_break" case carries NEL, U+2028 or U+2029, which are line breaks to a YAML 1.1 parser and ordinary characters to a YAML 1.2 one; both reference readers refuse it at LOAD, on the text, before any YAML parse, and the refusal names the case's "code_point" and "line". A SPLITTER is not the gate for that kind: the grammar has a perfectly good answer for those bytes (they are not line breaks and no block starts there), and the case in splits/ that proves it is kept, marked "loadable": false. "writes", meaningful only when "loads" is true, says whether a writer that preserves the flow block's SOURCE BYTES can write the document back; a canonical writer that has no source slice at all (the Python reference's dumps()) is not bound by it. not_delimitable: documents that split perfectly well but whose flow node the grammar cannot delimit, because it is not written as a bare `flow:` key line at column zero (a flow-style document, or `flow :`). Every reader LOADS them, the split simply produces no 'flow' key, and a source-slice writer MUST refuse to write them back: the block's bytes were never captured, so the only alternatives are dropping the block or emitting a re-serialisation in the place the source text belongs.

  name: demo
flow:
  # a comment

splits.note: The CR is removed to decide whether a line is a key line, and kept in the slice. An implementation that anchors with ECMAScript's . instead of [^\n] fails the key line 'flow: value\r' here.

splits.name: unicode_line_separator_inside_a_scalar_is_not_a_line_break
splits.doc:
format_version: "1.0"
assembly:
  name: "demo flow: injected"
flow:
  steps: []
splits.note: assembly.name carries U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR followed by `flow: injected`, all inside one double-quoted scalar. The grammar defines a line as LF-terminated with one optional preceding CR and nothing else, so there is no line break there and no key line: the whole scalar stays in the assembly block. An implementation that splits with Python's str.splitlines(), which also breaks on CR, VT, FF, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029, grows a `flow` block that is not in the file and hands a foreign host a block whose bytes came out of somebody's assembly name. That is the whole case, and it is why both reference readers iterate on LF by hand. The split verdict above is unchanged and is why this case stays here. The LOAD verdict is not the same question and it moved: U+2028 anywhere in a document is now ill-formed, so both reference readers refuse THIS document at load too, which is what "loadable": false records. Keeping the case is the point: the grammar must still not grow a `flow` block out of a scalar, and a reader refusing the document is not a splitter agreeing with it.

refuse.name: double_quoted_key_at_column_zero
refuse.reason: A splitter attaches "flow": and its body to the assembly block, where the exporter owns them and regenerates them away on the next export. Refuse instead of mis-attributing.

refuse.name: single_quoted_key_at_column_zero
refuse.reason: Same guard for the single-quoted spelling.

refuse.name: quoted_key_at_column_zero_without_a_flow_block
refuse.reason: The guard is about block ownership, not about flow: a document with a quoted key at column zero is refused whether or not it carries a flow block. This is the spelling a document-wide key-quoting emitter switch produces (validation rule 7).

refuse.name: repeated_top_level_key_is_ill_formed
refuse.doc:
format_version: "1.0"
assembly:
  name: demo
flow:
  steps: []
netlist:
  nets: []
flow:
  extra: true
refuse.reason: A document names each top-level key once. This one names flow twice, and there is no reading of it that is conforming: PyYAML resolves the key to the LAST value, yaml-cpp to the FIRST, so two conforming readers build different documents from these bytes. The splitter could concatenate the runs without dropping a byte, which is what it used to do, but that only decides who owns the text and not which value wins, and neither the schema nor a parsed node tree can see that anything happened. Refused on the text, at load, by every reader.

refuse.name: next_line_smuggles_a_top_level_key
refuse.doc:
format_version: "1.0"
assembly:
  name: demoformat_version: "9.0"
components: []
refuse.reason: PyYAML 6.0.3 reads NEL (U+0085) as a line break (YAML 1.1), so the `format_version: "9.0"` that follows it becomes a SECOND top-level key: safe_load returns format_version '9.0' while the top-level key list is unchanged, so the spoof moves a VALUE and not the shape and a "no unexpected keys" check does not see it. yaml-cpp 0.8.0 (YAML 1.2) throws "illegal map value" on the same bytes. Two conforming readers, two different documents, so the text is refused before either parser sees it.

refuse.name: next_line_inside_a_plain_scalar
refuse.reason: The same separator followed by ordinary text flips the disagreement: yaml-cpp 0.8.0 LOADS this document with the NEL (U+0085) bytes kept inside the scalar and PyYAML 6.0.3 throws a ScannerError. Parity is broken in BOTH directions and which reader refuses depends on the payload, which is why the rule is a text-level refusal in both readers and not one reader imitating the other.

not_delimitable.name: flow_style_document_has_no_delimitable_flow_block
not_delimitable.reason: A whole document written in flow style. YAML reads a flow node from it and the grammar sees one line that is not a key line, so the block has no slice. The document loads; writing it back would have to invent the bytes.
